title: what is the minimum amount of code needed for a  3D FPS /TPS style multiplayer game with weapons and items?
author: Standard-Fisherman-5
selftext: my current gameplay affecting code file corpus sits at 36K lines, and im wondering what is the absolute minimum needed for something like say, quake or something. I am using C++ with server relay internals in Lua. I know quake 3 was around 250K but that was all in C plus it's old and has a lot more features like matchmaking which I don't need yet.

comments.author: Reasonable_Run_6724
comments.body: If you are gonna make your own engine then 100-200k is a reasonable amount on c++, if you make it on python for example you may reach as low as 60k, but you will need to optimize a lot to reach anywhere close to c++ performance.

replies.author: Standard-Fisherman-5
replies.body: my renderer is around 4k, physics around 3k, and I have a giant godlike just called game.cpp that is 12k. my server\_tick.cpp was around 3k before I switched to Lua. its an authoritative server model with snapshot physics tick at 30hz but transporter issues make it less, and I gutted all of my client side interpolation and reconciliation because it was way too difficult to debug and any tiny modification in gameplay code lead to bug hunting whackamole that kept me stuck forever. now its working and I can actually debug stuff but the con is that server owns global state and there's stutter due to each snapshot refreshing into a discrete position. I tried making interpolation server side so I could keep the authoritative server integrity intact but even that introduced bugs that prevented effective melleee combat, mysterious disappearances of remote players, wrong direction presentation and it was too much. im just trying to simplify even more. because even with vibe coding I need to be able to read and trace the exact control flow because agents just LOVE to constantly add new surfaces and bloatware and entropy max and I've never been able to control it aside unless I review everything meaning the codebase needs to be small and simple enough to where I can actually understand what the code does in end to end.

replies.author: Reasonable_Run_6724
replies.body: Just remember that all the graphical passes and vfx or many particle features may make a lot of complexity code wize. Just the UI alone took me around 13k of pure code.

replies.author: Standard-Fisherman-5
replies.body: I guess then I should focus on making codebase more readable, believe it or not my world.cpp used to be included in game.cpp, and Ive been conscious about modularity as much as I can.  I have stripped all potential mixed ownership paths, use shared modules anywhere I can, basically stripped the UI down to almost nothing.

replies.author: Reasonable_Run_6724
replies.body: Tell me about it, currently i have around 45 python files (i keep two scripts for shaders - one for 3d and screen passes, the second for UI slicing)

comments.author: -Dargs
comments.body: If you use a language that has semicolon statement terminators you could write the whole thing in 1 line.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body: How do you handle test automation?

replies.author: Standard-Fisherman-5
replies.body: I have a JavaScript watchdog file corpus decoupled from actual runtime game binary. I use playwright to simulate choreography/mouse key inputs for all actions independently, while a separate set of global/local state recorders for tab 1 tab2 and vps server state recordings per run. So 3 game time families of artifacts plus a VPS journal that captures server machine health and network transport data etc per run. I also use a render oracle for each tab to catch visual bugs which lives inside each client side recorders bundle, and I have additional manual visual mode that screen records the two tabs and stitches the recording side by side with exact timestamps per tick so I can visually confirm artifacts. The server global state recorder and client side artifact recorders are all locked via per run slot manifest that can’t start until my work tree is committed and not dirty. That way every run is locked with a rollbackable codebase state snapshot and safety tag. I have a master watchdog runner python wrapper that automatically commits, resets the server and rebuilds all the game files, starts recording and captures all 3 families per tick and outputs a giant json dump. That json dump is fed into an analyze_run.py with a bunch of fuzzy parsing and other analysis functions that  I use to debug and  compare runs and it automatically compares code diffs via git. I also have a giant “failure log” that keeps track of bugs,  failure families, fix attempts, and even process failures. The analyze_run.py automatically adds to the failure log after each run, and I can use the script to debug, view previous attempts and triage the failure log runtime artifacts  related to the bug family, compare exact file by file line changes, process failures etc. for example, if I’m currently stuck on a z slight jitter bug I can fuzzy search “z jitter” and it spits out all matching runs, failure log entries, dailed and previous fix attempts, associated bug families and pass fail gates etc and if I want to look further I can compare tick by tick the global state machine. Since it’s strictly decoupled from game binary, updating the watchdog to add new probes won’t contaminate the game codebase state and vice versa. I also have two servers, one for live release and a debug server and I can push to live release version with one command.

replies.author: AgenticGameDev
replies.body: That is epic! Do you have any post about this or blog which is mor in depth? I use heavy AI TDD but this is a completely different approach as I use Unity and much more rigged validation of always passing test and more of a test driven design. This is more of a heuristic aproch?

replies.author: Standard-Fisherman-5
replies.body: No I don’t but I’ll definitely do that once it ships. It’s basically the Ralph loop workflow that happened naturally after many many many failures. Like the failure log was what started it all (it’s now 20K + lines over the last 4 months) every bug fix led to a new bug or regression I was playing constant whack a mole and refactoring over and over, each time the codebase kept getting bloated and after a certain point I couldn’t read my own code base which made me have to delete it all, after a certain point any new bug fix attempt was already tried in some way. I literally have 4 partial abandoned refactoring port attempts, 1 for godot, one for unity, one in pure javascript one in rust/bevy. Each time I kept running into the same process failures and bug patterns until I finally cobbled together a progressable system and that’s when the phase shift occurred from spinning my wheels to iterative progress. I’ve made many projects along the way but this custom game engine and multiplayer server has definitely taken the longest out of all of them. I guess the generalized workflow that I have now for all of my projects would be: 1. Keep codebase and knowledge base as physically small, readable and simple as possible, for each project I now have the failure log plus a spec document and that’s it. Everything else is archived/non canonical and is dumpstered after each session. My commit hook makes it so that any other loose file must be deleted before any run and I have a code ceiling so any additional lines of code must be met with equal deletions unless I explicitly bypass. 2. All Tests must be decoupled from the code you are testing AND must be user reachable AND all test outputs must be machine readable(no screenshots, no heuristic, no “uploading screenshot image to an lllm” etc. ) and any semantic extraction must sit on top of this machine readable/deterministic test output layer. That’s the most general way I can put it. Like you know those automatic piano machines that they use to have in the Wild West movies where you have holes in a roll of paper and you feed it into a giant key pressing machine that sits on top of a normal piano and you feed the music roll and it just presses the keys? That’s kind of what needs to happen for any test I make now for any project. The automatic piano player machine is completely separate and decoupled from the piano itself, it’s programmable, and all probing actions are user reachable. For example, I made a custom sprite sheet slicer and editor, and I set up the automated testing in the same way I described above for my watchdog corpus for the multiplayer server. First I mapped all the UI buttons in a giant spec table with each button having an associated state, action and expected response/output. Then I have a set of goal sprite sheet images and made a recipe generator script that took 2 inputs: 1. the goal sprite sheet image pixel by pixel from left to right top to buttom and 2nd input: the UI spec table. Both are  fed in through the recipe generator script that spits out a randomized recipe  of the exact sequence of UI button presses  that needs to be pressed and the expected image and editor state at each step in order to make the pixel by pixel match of the goal sprite sheet using the sprite sheet editor from a blank file, and the sequence of steps/ recipe is random each time. I use playwright to perform the recipe steps on the editor and a single run is an attempt of executing the recipe through playwright that executes the recipe dictated mouse and key press in the sequence given by the recipe generator.  I have a separate, third global editor state recorder that records the editor state at each recipe step, the state of the sprite sheet image being created in the editor at each step per action, and the final json dump will include both the expected sprite sheet image state from the recipe generator and editor image state per step in the recipe from the editor state recorder. of course the first 100 tests will always fail, with first 50+ not even reaching the end of the recipe. But for each failure, the failure points and tested output file/partial state  gets recorded, the test output is deterministic and machine readable by agents, and all are seperate, rollbackable, and modifiable so I can test new  feartures by adding additional entries into the input spec table that the recipe generator takes in, change the editor(main codebase), change/enhance the editor recorder, and  change/enhance the recipe generator/playwright script all independently without risk of contaminating each other. This allows automation of output triage, iterative bug logging and fix attempts without having to play whackamole and managing constant agent process failures mentioned above. the agent builds the editor feature/bug fix, runs the unified testing routine wrapper which commits the attempt -> calls recipe generator, -> test run occurs end to end -> output json dump -> auto appended and indexed in the failure log via analyze_run.py -> agent reads the output, uses the analyze_run.py itself to in the debugging process instead of constant token gobbling bash commands, making scanning the code base,  code diffs, previous runs, more context  efficient and accurate -> plans and applies fixes -> repeat.  As the failure log builds up along with previous recipe test attempts, you build up your analyze_runs.py with more and more bug family groupings,  parsing commands, secondary semantic indexes, etc automatically. After a critical threshold the process kind of bootstraps itself to where I don’t have to do too much except review and approve plans and bug closures.

replies.author: AgenticGameDev
replies.body: And you feel the architecture still is solid? I feel I need to handhold so much to keep the ai from screwing up with bad architecture…

replies.author: Standard-Fisherman-5
replies.body: Yeah I am in the same boat tbh, but yes finally, partly due to the constant refactor I learned a lot, partly from keeping a eagle eye on the edits to scanning agent proposals, and I also keep a hand written control flow maps lol but yeah If I don’t pay attention it definitely will become bloated and unreadable easily. But hooks and guard scripts and regular audit passes and making test results readable to the agents helped so much.

replies.author: AgenticGameDev
replies.body: Sounds like you have much more hands off. I have 5 strict guidelines + I do spend about 1-4h planning before I’m happy with the ai plan for a 1.5k-2.5k LOC new module.
